Tight Competitive Bounds for Online Matching on Forests

Bartłomiej Bosek    Grzegorz Gutowski    Paweł Putra    Anna Zych-Pawlewicz
Abstract

We study the online matching problem, its fractional relaxation, and the fractional online vertex cover problem on forests whose edges arrive one at a time in an arbitrary order. Matching decisions are irrevocable, and vertex-cover weights can only increase over time. For online matching, we present a randomized algorithm with expected competitive ratio 4/74/7 against an oblivious adversary, improving the previous 5/95/9 guarantee. We also present a deterministic algorithm that simultaneously maintains a 4/74/7-competitive fractional matching and a 7/47/4-competitive fractional vertex cover. This deterministic algorithm improves the previous 5/95/9 guarantee for fractional matching and the 11/611/6 guarantee for fractional vertex cover. We prove that 4/74/7 is optimal for both randomized and fractional matching, even on growing trees of maximum degree four.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider the matching problem in the online edge arrival model. In this model, the vertex set is known in advance and edges arrive one at a time. Each edge must be accepted or rejected upon arrival. The algorithm maintains a set of edges forming a matching, i.e., no two selected edges share an endpoint. The objective is to maximize the (expected) size of the matching, and the challenge is that the decisions of the algorithm are irrevocable, i.e., once an edge is added to the matching, it must remain there for the whole runtime of the algorithm. For this reason, we cannot hope to maintain an offline-optimal matching at every time step. Instead, we aim for a competitive ratio as close to 11 as possible, i.e., a guarantee that the expected size of our matching is at least this fraction of the offline optimum.

A greedy deterministic algorithm guarantees a solution half the size of a maximum matching, and there is no hope for a deterministic algorithm to beat the competitive ratio of 12\frac{1}{2} even on a path of length three. Thus, the question of whether one could beat the ratio of 12\frac{1}{2} using randomization was a central open question in the area for a long time. Recently Gamlath, Kapralov, Maggiori, Svensson and Wajc [12] showed that we cannot hope for that either, even on bipartite graphs.

This motivates studying the edge arrival model on more restricted classes of graphs. The most widely considered restriction in the literature is to forests. The pessimistic online bounds for deterministic algorithms also apply to this class; however, we can achieve better guarantees for randomized algorithms. Buchbinder, Segev and Tkach gave a randomized algorithm with competitive ratio 59≈0.5556\frac{5}{9}\approx 0.5556 [9, 10] and proved that this guarantee is optimal within their Min-Index framework. Their upper bound for unrestricted algorithms is approximately 0.59140.5914, even on trees of maximum degree three. We close this gap at 4/7≈0.57144/7\approx 0.5714. Our algorithm handles arbitrary edge orders, whereas the matching upper bound already holds on growing trees: after the initial edge, each arrival attaches a new leaf to the existing tree.

In pursuit of this goal, we study the fractional online matching and the fractional vertex cover problem on forests in the edge arrival model. In the fractional online matching problem, each arriving edge receives an irrevocable weight from [0,1][0,1], so that at any vertex the weights of adjacent edges sum up to at most one. The objective is to maximize the sum of the assigned weights. In the fractional vertex cover problem, vertices receive weights from [0,1][0,1] so that every presented edge is covered, i.e., the weights assigned to its endpoints sum up to at least one. The objective is to minimize the total weight of the vertices, and the decisions are irrevocable in the sense that we may only ever increase the weights assigned to the vertices from one step to the next. For the matching, a competitive ratio c≤1c\leq 1 means that after every edge arrival the weight of the matching is at least cc times the offline optimum, whereas for the vertex cover a competitive ratio of c≥1c\geq 1 means that the weight of the vertex cover is at most cc times the optimum.

Fractional matching and fractional vertex cover are linear-programming duals, and their offline optima coincide. The online requirements are different, however: matching weights are fixed at arrival, whereas cover weights must remain nondecreasing as constraints are revealed. An offline dual certificate in the analysis of a fractional online matching algorithm does not immediately translate to an online fractional vertex cover algorithm. Indeed, for fractional matching on forests, the result of Buchbinder, Segev and Tkach [10] implies a 59\frac{5}{9}-competitive algorithm, while for fractional vertex cover on forests, Baligács et al. [1] obtain an 11/6≈1.833311/6\approx 1.8333-competitive algorithm under edge arrivals. The two algorithms differ substantially. Both solutions [10, 1] use weak duality in the analysis, but neither constructs a fractional matching and a fractional vertex cover at the same time in an online manner.

We improve both of the results above with one online algorithm, which constructs both a fractional online matching and a fractional online vertex cover at the same time, providing competitive ratios of 47≈0.5714\frac{4}{7}\approx 0.5714 and 74=1.75\frac{7}{4}=1.75, respectively. We show that no algorithm achieves a constant competitive ratio of c>47c>\frac{4}{7} for fractional matching. This also implies that no randomized online matching algorithm achieves an expected competitive ratio of c>47c>\frac{4}{7}, as we discuss in the next section. Our hard instance is a growing tree, implying the same hardness in the easier vertex arrival model, and thus establishing tight competitive ratios for the online matching in the vertex arrival model on forests as well.

For matching, we also show how to adapt the fractional algorithm to obtain a randomized online algorithm with the same competitive ratio.

Our results.

We prove the following guarantees.

Theorem 1.

In the edge arrival model on forests, there is a deterministic algorithm that simultaneously maintains a 4/74/7-competitive fractional matching and a 7/47/4-competitive fractional vertex cover.

Theorem 2.

In the edge arrival model on forests, there is a randomized online matching algorithm with expected competitive ratio 4/74/7 against an oblivious adversary.

Theorem 3.

For every constant c>4/7c>4/7 there is a growing tree of maximum degree four on which no fractional or randomized online matching algorithm is cc-competitive.

Outline.

Section 2 summarizes related work. Section 3 defines the problems and the arrival model. Section 4 provides and analyzes the algorithm for both fractional problems. Section 5 constructs and analyzes the randomized matching algorithm. Section 6 proves the matching hardness.

2 Related work

The online matching problem dates back to the breakthrough work of Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani [14] in 1990. The authors studied online matching in an easier one-sided vertex arrival model on bipartite graphs. This setting and its generalizations have applications in ad auctions [7]. In the vertex arrival model, the vertices arrive one at a time together with all the edges connecting to the vertices presented so far. The one-sided version assumes that only the vertices on one side of the bipartition arrive in an online fashion, while the vertices on the other side are known up front to the algorithm. Due to the upper bound of 12\frac{1}{2} for the competitive ratio of any deterministic algorithm, the authors in [14] turn to randomization and show a widely celebrated Ranking algorithm, which admits a (tight) competitive ratio of (1−1/e)≈0.6321(1-1/e)\approx 0.6321. The Ranking algorithm was further studied in several more works [3, 11], resulting in a relatively simple primal-dual analysis [11] that provided the basis for future work. Fractional online matching was also studied in the one-sided vertex arrival model, resulting in an elegant water filling algorithm with a (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-competitive ratio [7]. The water-filling algorithm constructs a feasible dual solution online; for Ranking, the dual variables are also constructed online, but feasibility holds in expectation.

Wang and Wong [19] studied the dual fractional vertex cover problem under vertex arrivals and observed that it generalizes the ski-rental problem. If one restricts vertex weights to {0,1}\{0,1\}, thus obtaining the integral online vertex cover problem, one immediately hits a tight competitive ratio of 22 for deterministic algorithms, attained by a simple greedy algorithm [4, 5]. Wang and Wong [19] provide an e/(e−1)≈1.5820e/(e-1)\approx 1.5820-competitive algorithm for the fractional variant in the one-sided vertex arrival model. This competitive ratio is the reciprocal of the (1−1e)(1-\frac{1}{e}) ratio of the Ranking algorithm. Their algorithm constructs the vertex cover and the matching simultaneously, and the competitive ratio follows naturally from weak duality. More interestingly, the algorithm of Wang and Wong [19] can be applied to the general vertex arrival model, where it achieves a competitive ratio of 1Γ≈1.9008\frac{1}{\Gamma}\approx 1.9008 for the fractional online vertex cover problem, while the best known lower bound is approximately 1.82441.8244 [15]. As a byproduct, from the primal-dual analysis Wang and Wong derive a competitive ratio of Γ≈0.5261\Gamma\approx 0.5261 for the fractional online matching problem in the general vertex arrival model, later shown tight by Tang [18]. Subsequently, Gamlath, Kapralov, Maggiori, Svensson and Wajc [12] show how to round the weights produced by the algorithm of Wang and Wong to obtain a randomized algorithm for the online matching problem in the general vertex arrival model, achieving a competitive ratio strictly larger than 12\frac{1}{2}, thus answering a long-standing open problem.

The edge arrival model turns out to be substantially harder for the algorithm. In the same paper [12], it was shown that there is no algorithm for online fractional matching achieving a competitive ratio larger than 12\frac{1}{2} by any constant. Hardness for fractional online matching immediately implies the same hardness for randomized online matching: every randomized online matching induces a fractional one by assigning each edge its probability of being selected. The converse is more delicate: Buchbinder, Naor and Wajc [8] study the constraints that make lossless rounding possible. Just recently, Tang and Zhang showed that also for the fractional vertex cover problem under edge arrivals one cannot hope for a competitive ratio smaller than 22 [17], even on bipartite graphs. These hardness results make structural restrictions essential for improving the competitive guarantees under edge arrivals.

Buchbinder, Segev and Tkach [10] established a 59≈0.5556\frac{5}{9}\approx 0.5556-competitive randomized online matching algorithm for forests. Taking the probabilities of accepting the edges as their weights yields a fractional algorithm with the same guarantee. Their Min-Index framework maintains an ordered collection of matchings. Each arriving edge is added to the first matching that can accept it, or rejected if none can. The output matching is chosen according to probabilities fixed in advance. They show that no instantiation of this framework achieves a competitive ratio greater than 59\frac{5}{9} on forests. For graphs of maximum degree dd known in advance, they also give a deterministic algorithm that maintains a fractional matching and a fractional vertex cover simultaneously online, with competitive ratio 12​(1+12d−1)\frac{1}{2}\bigl(1+\frac{1}{2^{d}-1}\bigr) for matching and its reciprocal for vertex cover. For d=3d=3 this gives 47\frac{4}{7} and 74\frac{7}{4}, respectively, but the matching guarantee tends to 12\frac{1}{2} as dd grows.

Buchbinder, Segev and Tkach [10] also give a hardness bound for fractional matching of 49−5≈0.5914\frac{4}{9-\sqrt{5}}\approx 0.5914 which holds already for growing trees with maximum degree three. Pashkovich and Snow [16] subsequently attained this bound for fractional online matching on all graphs of maximum degree three, thus closing the problem of fractional online matching for this class of graphs. They also show that no randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio larger than 0.58070.5807 on graphs of maximum degree three, and no fractional algorithm achieves a competitive ratio larger than 0.58890.5889 on graphs of maximum degree four. Our results determine the optimal fractional and randomized ratios for forests without degree restrictions. Moreover, our upper bound for fractional matching on forests improves the upper bound of [16] within the class of graphs of maximum degree four, as our construction is in fact a growing tree of maximum degree four. For fractional vertex cover on forests under edge arrivals [1] gave an 116\frac{11}{6}-competitive algorithm, which our algorithm improves to 74\frac{7}{4}.

Bromblik [6] established a lower bound of (9−5)/4≈1.6910(9-\sqrt{5})/4\approx 1.6910 for online fractional vertex cover on trees under edge arrivals. Together with our 7/47/4-competitive algorithm, this leaves a gap between (9−5)/4(9-\sqrt{5})/4 and 7/47/4 for the optimal competitive ratio.

In [1] the authors consider the fractional vertex cover problem also in the incremental model, when the entire edge arrival sequence is known in advance. For that model, they prove an optimal ratio of 3/23/2. Our hardness bound for fractional matching applies also in the incremental model, proving that even if the entire future is known in advance, the fractional matching algorithm still cannot be better than 47\frac{4}{7}-competitive.

Independently of our work, Bienkowski [2] developed an algorithm for forests under edge arrivals that simultaneously maintains a fractional vertex cover and a fractional matching, with competitive ratios 4−5≈1.76394-\sqrt{5}\approx 1.7639 and 1/(4−5)≈0.56691/(4-\sqrt{5})\approx 0.5669, respectively. Our fractional algorithm improves these guarantees to 7/4=1.757/4=1.75 and 4/7≈0.57144/7\approx 0.5714, respectively.

There has been work on online matching on forests with free disposal, where one is allowed to discard edges previously accepted to the matching. In this model, Jiang and Zhang [13] obtained the optimal randomized ratio 23\frac{2}{3} on growing trees, and a randomized ratio 58\frac{5}{8} on general forests. These guarantees do not apply to the irrevocable decisions that we consider in this paper.

3 Preliminaries

For a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), a matching is a set of edges with disjoint endpoints, and a vertex cover is a set of vertices containing at least one endpoint of every edge. A fractional matching 𝐱\mathbf{x} assigns weight xe∈[0,1]x_{e}\in[0,1] to each edge ee such that ∑e∋vxe≤1\sum_{e\ni v}x_{e}\leq 1 for every vertex vv; its value is ∑e∈Exe\sum_{e\in E}x_{e}. A fractional vertex cover 𝐲\mathbf{y} assigns weight yv∈[0,1]y_{v}\in[0,1] to each vertex vv such that every edge u​vuv is covered, meaning yu+yv≥1y_{u}+y_{v}\geq 1; its cost is ∑v∈Vyv\sum_{v\in V}y_{v}. On forests, all four problems have the same optimum value, by Kőnig’s theorem and weak duality.

We consider randomized algorithms for matching and deterministic algorithms for fractional matching and fractional vertex cover.

In the online edge arrival model, an oblivious adversary fixes a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and an edge order e1,…,eme_{1},\dots,e_{m} in advance. The algorithm knows VV and receives the edges one at a time. After arrival tt, it must maintain a feasible solution for Gt:=(V,{e1,…,et})G_{t}:=(V,\left\{e_{1},\dots,e_{t}\right\}), using only the revealed prefix and its own random choices.

Matching decisions are made upon arrival and are irrevocable: the maintained matching MtM_{t} satisfies Mt−1⊆Mt⊆Mt−1∪{et}M_{t-1}\subseteq M_{t}\subseteq M_{t-1}\cup\{e_{t}\}, with M0=∅M_{0}=\emptyset. A fractional matching algorithm assigns each arriving edge an irrevocable weight xex_{e}. A fractional vertex-cover algorithm maintains vertex weights yvy_{v} that start at zero and can only increase.

The objective is to maximize matching cardinality or fractional matching value, or to minimize fractional vertex-cover cost. Write ALGt\mathrm{ALG}_{t} for the cardinality, value, or cost of the maintained solution and OPTt\mathrm{OPT}_{t} for the corresponding offline optimum on GtG_{t}. An algorithm is cc-competitive if, for every input and every t∈{1,…,m}t\in\left\{1,\dots,m\right\},

𝔼⁡[ALGt]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{ALG}_{t}] ≥c⋅OPTt\displaystyle\geq c\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{t} for matching,\displaystyle\text{for matching,}
ALGt\displaystyle\mathrm{ALG}_{t} ≥c⋅OPTt\displaystyle\geq c\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{t} for fractional matching,\displaystyle\text{for fractional matching,}
ALGt\displaystyle\mathrm{ALG}_{t} ≤c⋅OPTt\displaystyle\leq c\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{t} for fractional vertex cover.\displaystyle\text{for fractional vertex cover.}

The expectation is over the algorithm’s random choices.

4 Fractional algorithm

Our algorithm is based on linear programming duality between fractional matching and fractional vertex cover. Recall that the fractional matching problem on a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is the linear program on the left, and the fractional vertex cover problem is its dual, on the right:

max∑e∈Exes.t.∑e∋vxe≤1for all ​v∈V​,xe≥0for all ​e∈E​,min∑v∈Vyvs.t.yu+yv≥1for all ​u​v∈E​,yv≥0for all ​v∈V​.\begin{array}[]{r@{\quad}l}\max&\sum_{e\in E}x_{e}\\[2.0pt] \text{s.t.}&\sum_{e\ni v}x_{e}\leq 1\quad\text{for all }v\in V\text{,}\\[2.0pt] &x_{e}\geq 0\quad\text{for all }e\in E\text{,}\end{array}\qquad\qquad\begin{array}[]{r@{\quad}l}\min&\sum_{v\in V}y_{v}\\[2.0pt] \text{s.t.}&y_{u}+y_{v}\geq 1\quad\text{for all }uv\in E\text{,}\\[2.0pt] &y_{v}\geq 0\quad\text{for all }v\in V\text{.}\end{array}

Observe that every optimal solution of either linear program assigns weights at most 11. By weak duality, the value of every fractional matching of GG is at most the cost of every fractional vertex cover of GG.

The previous 5/95/9-competitive matching algorithm of Buchbinder, Segev and Tkach [10] and the 11/611/6-competitive vertex cover algorithm of [1] use duality to prove their competitive guarantees. In these analyses, the dual solution serves as a proof certificate; it is not maintained as a second online solution. The certificates are constructed for each input prefix, and their evolution need not satisfy the online constraints. For example, in the analysis of the matching algorithm of [10], the dual vertex cover may decrease vertex weights when two trees are joined. Such decreases violate the online vertex-cover constraints, so this certificate does not yield an online vertex-cover algorithm [17]. Our algorithm uses duality in a stronger, constructive sense: it maintains valid online solutions for both the fractional matching and the fractional vertex cover. At every input prefix, each solution certifies the competitive guarantee of the other. Specifically, for a fixed constant c∈(0,1]c\in(0,1], the maintained fractional matching 𝐱\mathbf{x} and fractional vertex cover 𝐲\mathbf{y} satisfy the dual inequality

∑e∈E⁡(Gt)xe≥c⋅∑v∈Vyvfor every ​t​.\sum_{e\in E(G_{t})}x_{e}\ \geq\ c\cdot\sum_{v\in V}y_{v}\qquad\text{for every }t\text{.} (1)

Since GtG_{t} is a forest, the matching and vertex-cover linear programs applied to GtG_{t} have integral optimal solutions and optimum value OPTt\mathrm{OPT}_{t}. Weak duality and (1) give

c⋅OPTt≤c⋅∑v∈Vyv≤∑e∈E⁡(Gt)xe≤OPTt​.c\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{t}\ \leq\ c\cdot\sum_{v\in V}y_{v}\ \leq\ \sum_{e\in E(G_{t})}x_{e}\ \leq\ \mathrm{OPT}_{t}\text{.}

Hence the matching is cc-competitive and the cover is 1c\frac{1}{c}-competitive.

At any time tt, let the load mvm_{v} of a vertex vv be the total matching weight assigned to revealed edges incident to vv, i.e., mv:=∑e∈E⁡(Gt):e∋vxem_{v}:=\sum_{e\in E(G_{t}):\,e\ni v}x_{e}. The crucial idea behind our approach is to relate the two solutions at every vertex, so that the weight yvy_{v} of a vertex vv in the cover is a function of its load mvm_{v}. For that purpose, we define a cover function ψ:[0,1]→[0,1]\psi\colon[0,1]\to[0,1] so that yv=ψ⁡(mv)y_{v}=\psi(m_{v}). Under the conditions of Lemma 4, we define the match function χ:[0,1]2→[0,1]\chi\colon[0,1]^{2}\to[0,1] for a,b∈[0,1]a,b\in[0,1] by

χ⁡(a,b):=min⁡{x∈[0,1−max⁡{a,b}]:ψ⁡(a+x)+ψ⁡(b+x)≥1}​.\chi(a,b):=\min\left\{x\in[0,1-\max\{a,b\}]:\psi(a+x)+\psi(b+x)\geq 1\right\}\text{.} (2)

We can then use the cover function ψ\psi and the match function χ\chi to define Algorithm 1 – an online algorithm for fractional matching and vertex cover.

The analysis of Algorithm 1 is organized as follows. First, in Lemma 4, we give conditions on the cover function ψ\psi under which the match function χ\chi is well-defined and the algorithm maintains valid online solutions. Next, in Lemma 5, we give sufficient conditions on the cover function under which the dual inequality in Equation 1 holds for Algorithm 1 and a fixed c∈(0,1]c\in(0,1]. Finally, we define an explicit cover function ψ⋆\psi^{\star} and verify that it satisfies the conditions. Applying both lemmas, we obtain the competitive guarantees.

Lemma 4.

Suppose that ψ:[0,1]→[0,1]\psi\colon[0,1]\to[0,1] is continuous and nondecreasing, with ψ⁡(0)=0\psi(0)=0 and ψ⁡(1)=1\psi(1)=1. Then Algorithm 1 maintains a valid online fractional matching and a valid online fractional vertex cover after every edge arrival.

Proof.

Fix any a,b∈[0,1]a,b\in[0,1]. Put h=1−max⁡{a,b}h=1-\max\{a,b\}. Then h∈[0,1]h\in[0,1], a+h,b+h∈[0,1]a+h,b+h\in[0,1], and at least one of a+h,b+ha+h,b+h equals 11. Since ψ⁡(1)=1\psi(1)=1 and ψ\psi is nonnegative, x=hx=h satisfies all constraints in Equation 2, so the feasible set is nonempty. The function x↦ψ⁡(a+x)+ψ⁡(b+x)x\mapsto\psi(a+x)+\psi(b+x) is continuous and nondecreasing on [0,h][0,h]. Thus the feasible set is a nonempty closed subset of the compact interval [0,h][0,h], and the minimum in Equation 2 is attained. Thus, the value χ⁡(a,b)\chi(a,b) is well-defined.

The initialization and update rules in Algorithm 1 ensure that mv=∑e∈E⁡(Gt):e∋vxem_{v}=\sum_{e\in E(G_{t}):\,e\ni v}x_{e} and yv=ψ⁡(mv)y_{v}=\psi(m_{v}) for every vertex vv after tt arrivals. The value of xex_{e} for an edge ee never changes once it is assigned when ee arrives.

All loads are initially zero. For 𝐱\mathbf{x} to be a valid online fractional matching, it remains to prove that all loads remain in [0,1][0,1] after every arrival. For an arriving edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v), let a=mua=m_{u} and b=mvb=m_{v} be its old endpoint loads. For a,b∈[0,1]a,b\in[0,1], the definition of χ\chi guarantees that xe=χ⁡(a,b)x_{e}=\chi(a,b) satisfies xe≥0x_{e}\geq 0, a+xe≤1a+x_{e}\leq 1, and b+xe≤1b+x_{e}\leq 1. The algorithm increases the endpoint loads to a+xe,b+xea+x_{e},b+x_{e} and leaves all other loads unchanged. Thus all loads remain in [0,1][0,1], and 𝐱\mathbf{x} remains a feasible solution.

The initial graph has no edges, so the initial vertex weights are zero and 𝐲\mathbf{y} is a valid online fractional vertex cover. For the same edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v), the updated endpoint weights sum to ψ⁡(a+xe)+ψ⁡(b+xe)\psi(a+x_{e})+\psi(b+x_{e}), which by the definition of χ\chi is at least 11, so the new edge is covered. Since loads only increase and ψ\psi is nondecreasing, vertex weights never decrease, and all earlier edges remain covered. Hence 𝐲\mathbf{y} is feasible after every arrival and satisfies the online constraints. ∎

Now, we give sufficient conditions on the cover function ψ\psi that ensure that the dual inequality in Equation 1 holds for a fixed c∈(0,1]c\in(0,1]. At any time tt, let TT be a component of the forest GtG_{t}. We define the surplus of TT by

S⁡(T):=∑e∈E⁡(T)xe−c⋅∑v∈V⁡(T)yv​.S(T):=\sum_{e\in E(T)}x_{e}-c\cdot\sum_{v\in V(T)}y_{v}\text{.}

In order to maintain the dual inequality in Equation 1, it would suffice to show that the surplus of any component is nonnegative. The surplus of a one-vertex component is 00. For other components, we fix a constant s≥0s\geq 0 and maintain a surplus of at least ss in every component containing at least one edge. An arriving edge in a forest joins two distinct components. We call it an isolated edge if both components are isolated vertices, a leaf edge if exactly one is an isolated vertex, and a join edge otherwise. Intuitively, adding an isolated edge must create surplus at least ss, adding a leaf edge must preserve it, and adding a join edge can decrease the combined surplus by at most ss.

Lemma 5.

Let ψ\psi satisfy the assumptions of Lemma 4, and let 0<c≤10<c\leq 1 and s≥0s\geq 0. Suppose that the weight xex_{e} chosen by Algorithm 1 for edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) with loads mu,mvm_{u},m_{v} before the arrival satisfies

xe≥{c+s,for an isolated edge,c⋅(1−ψ⁡(mu)),for a leaf edge with new vertex ​v​,c⋅max⁡{0,1−ψ⁡(mu)−ψ⁡(mv)}−s,for a join edge.x_{e}\geq\begin{cases}c+s,&\text{for an isolated edge,}\\[2.0pt] c\cdot\bigl(1-\psi(m_{u})\bigr),&\text{for a leaf edge with new vertex }v\text{,}\\[2.0pt] c\cdot\max\{0,1-\psi(m_{u})-\psi(m_{v})\}-s,&\text{for a join edge.}\end{cases} (3)

Then every component TT containing an edge satisfies S⁡(T)≥sS(T)\geq s at all times.

In particular, when the conditions of Lemma 5 are met, the algorithm maintains the dual inequality in Equation 1 for this choice of cc and ss and is therefore cc-competitive for fractional matching and 1c\frac{1}{c}-competitive for fractional vertex cover.

Proof.

We prove the bound by induction on the number of edges that have arrived. Initially every component is an isolated vertex and has surplus zero.

An arriving edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) joins two distinct components Tu,TvT_{u},T_{v} into a component TT. Let a=mua=m_{u}, b=mvb=m_{v} and put δ=max⁡{0,1−ψ⁡(a)−ψ⁡(b)}\delta=\max\{0,1-\psi(a)-\psi(b)\}. If ψ⁡(a)+ψ⁡(b)≥1\psi(a)+\psi(b)\geq 1, then xe=χ⁡(a,b)=0x_{e}=\chi(a,b)=0. 5 Randomized algorithm

We now use the cover function ψ⋆\psi^{\star} and its match function χ⋆\chi^{\star} to obtain a randomized online matching algorithm. For the analysis, we adapt the rounding argument of Jiang and Zhang [13]. Throughout this section, put c=47c=\frac{4}{7} and s=114s=\frac{1}{14}, as in Lemma 7. The algorithm maintains a matching MM and deterministic loads mvm_{v}, which will equal the probabilities that the vertices are matched. An arriving edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v) joins two distinct components of the forest. Since their random choices are independent and the old endpoint loads are a=mua=m_{u} and b=mvb=m_{v}, both endpoints are unmatched with probability (1−a)​(1−b)(1-a)(1-b). To accept ee with probability xex_{e}, we must have xe≤(1−a)​(1−b)x_{e}\leq(1-a)(1-b). The fractional weight χ⋆​(a,b)\chi^{\star}(a,b) can exceed this bound: for example,

χ⋆​(1314,114)=114>(1−1314)​(1−114)=13196​.\chi^{\star}\bigl(\tfrac{13}{14},\tfrac{1}{14}\bigr)=\tfrac{1}{14}>\bigl(1-\tfrac{13}{14}\bigr)\bigl(1-\tfrac{1}{14}\bigr)=\tfrac{13}{196}\text{.}

We therefore define the capped match function by

χˇ​(a,b)=min⁡{χ⋆​(a,b),(1−a)​(1−b)}​,\check{\chi}(a,b)=\min\{\chi^{\star}(a,b),(1-a)(1-b)\}\text{,} (6)

and we assign xe=χˇ​(a,b)x_{e}=\check{\chi}(a,b) to the edge. When both endpoints are unmatched, we accept the edge with probability xe/((1−a)​(1−b))x_{e}/((1-a)(1-b)). The loads increase by xex_{e} regardless of whether the edge is accepted.

The capped edge weights depend only on the revealed input, so the loads, which are sums of incident edge weights, are deterministic. We first prove that each load equals the probability that the corresponding vertex is matched. We then show that the capped weights satisfy the payment bounds in Equation 3 and use these bounds to maintain a surplus against every offline matching.

Lemma 8.

Algorithm 2 accepts each arriving edge ee with probability xex_{e}.

Proof.

All loads start at zero. For endpoint loads a,b∈[0,1]a,b\in[0,1], we have

0≤xe≤(1−a)​(1−b)≤min⁡{1−a,1−b}​,0\leq x_{e}\leq(1-a)(1-b)\leq\min\{1-a,1-b\}\text{,}

so the updated loads a+xea+x_{e} and b+xeb+x_{e} also lie in [0,1][0,1]. Assign an independent random variable to every arriving edge. The matching in a component depends only on the variables assigned to its own edges. Distinct components use disjoint sets of these variables, so their matchings are independent.

We prove by induction that each load mvm_{v} equals the probability that vv is matched. Initially all vertices are unmatched and all loads are zero. Suppose that e=(u,v)e=(u,v) arrives with old endpoint loads a,ba,b. Its endpoints lie in distinct components, so by independence and the induction hypothesis they are both unmatched with probability p=(1−a)​(1−b)p=(1-a)(1-b). If p>0p>0, the probability of accepting ee is p⋅(xe/p)=xep\cdot(x_{e}/p)=x_{e}. If p=0p=0, then xe=0x_{e}=0 and the edge is rejected. Since ee is accepted only when both endpoints are unmatched, their matching probabilities increase by xex_{e}, to a+xea+x_{e} and b+xeb+x_{e}, respectively. These are exactly the updated loads; all other loads and matching probabilities remain unchanged.∎

We now show that capping preserves the payment bounds in Equation 3. For isolated and leaf edges, the cap does not change the assigned weight. For join edges, it suffices to show that the cap (1−a)​(1−b)(1-a)(1-b) is itself large enough to satisfy the required payment bound. The following technical lemma gives the estimate needed for this step.

Lemma 9.

For all 0≤b≤a≤10\leq b\leq a\leq 1,

c⋅ψ⋆​(m)≥m2−114andc⋅ψ⋆​(m)≥m−37for every ​m∈[0,1]​.c\cdot\psi^{\star}(m)\geq\frac{m}{2}-\frac{1}{14}\qquad\text{and}\qquad c\cdot\psi^{\star}(m)\geq m-\frac{3}{7}\qquad\text{for every }m\in[0,1]\text{.}

=67−a+b2+a​b=1728+(12−a)​(12−b)≥1728≥12​.\displaystyle=\frac{6}{7}-\frac{a+b}{2}+ab=\frac{17}{28}+\left(\frac{1}{2}-a\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}-b\right)\geq\frac{17}{28}\geq\frac{1}{2}\text{.}

Lemma 7 establishes the payment bounds in Equation 3 for Algorithm 1 using ψ⋆\psi^{\star}. Its proof gives these bounds for arbitrary endpoint loads. We now show that capping preserves them, yielding the analogous guarantee for Algorithm 2.

Lemma 10.

For the cover function ψ⋆\psi^{\star}, the weights chosen by Algorithm 2 satisfy Equation 3 with c=47c=\frac{4}{7} and s=114s=\frac{1}{14}.

Proof.

We need to verify the three bounds in Equation 3 for isolated, leaf and join edges, with c=47c=\frac{4}{7} and s=114s=\frac{1}{14}.

  • •

    For an isolated edge, a=b=0a=b=0 and the cap is 11, so χˇ​(0,0)=χ⋆​(0,0)=μ⁡(0)=c+s\check{\chi}(0,0)=\chi^{\star}(0,0)=\mu(0)=c+s.

As before, put yv=ψ⋆​(mv)y_{v}=\psi^{\star}(m_{v}). Capping can leave an edge with yu+yv<1y_{u}+y_{v}<1, so these weights need not form a vertex cover. Let V⁡(ℳ)V(\mathcal{M}) be the set of vertices matched by ℳ\mathcal{M}, and define the matching surplus

S⁡(T,ℳ):=∑e∈E⁡(T)xe−c⋅(|ℳ|+∑v∈V⁡(T)∖V⁡(ℳ)yv)​.S(T,\mathcal{M}):=\sum_{e\in E(T)}x_{e}-c\cdot\left(|\mathcal{M}|+\sum_{v\in V(T)\setminus V(\mathcal{M})}y_{v}\right)\text{.}

The matching-surplus bound now allows us to prove the main result for randomized matching, which we restate below. See 2

Proof.

Algorithm 2 accepts only edges with two unmatched endpoints and never removes an accepted edge, so it maintains a valid online matching. By Lemma 8 and linearity of expectation,

𝔼⁡[|Mt|]=∑e∈E⁡(Gt)xe​.\mathbb{E}[|M_{t}|]=\sum_{e\in E(G_{t})}x_{e}\text{.}

6 Hardness for fractional matching in the edge arrival model

We now proceed to show our hardness result. We show in this section that any cc-competitive fractional online matching algorithm in the edge arrival model satisfies c≤4/7c\leq 4/7. We do so by constructing a family of growing trees of maximum degree four that rules out every competitive ratio greater than 4/74/7.

We move on to presenting the construction. The whole construction proceeds in 2​L+22L+2 stages, where LL is the parameter of our choice. As a result of applying the construction for parameter LL, we obtain a growing tree referred to as TLT_{L}. The construction starts with an initialization stage (Stage 00), then it proceeds through 2​L2L intermediate stages numbered from 11 to 2​L2L, ending up with a completion stage (Stage 2​L+12L+1). Each edge ee that we ever add to the tree is presented at a specific stage called stage⁡(e)\mathrm{stage}(e). After every two intermediate stages a new set of active vertices AℓA_{\ell} is exposed, used to proceed with the construction for the next two consecutive stages.

In the initialization stage 00, we present the first edge u​vuv and we set the active set A0={u,v}A_{0}=\{u,v\}, so both endpoints of the newly presented edge become active.

We proceed with the construction of the intermediate stages. For each ℓ∈{1,…,L}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,L\}, we define two consecutive stages: Stage 2​ℓ−12\ell-1 and Stage 2​ℓ2\ell. In Stage 2​ℓ−12\ell-1 we append a private pendant w′w^{\prime} to each active vertex w∈Aℓ−1w\in A_{\ell-1}. In Stage 2​ℓ2\ell, we append a private dummy vertex dwd_{w} to every active vertex w∈Aℓ−1w\in A_{\ell-1}, and to each previously added pendant w′w^{\prime} we append a private pendant w′′w^{\prime\prime}. Each pendant introduces a new edge to a vertex it is appended to. Finally, we declare a new set of active vertices Aℓ=⋃w∈Aℓ−1{w′,w′′}A_{\ell}=\bigcup_{w\in A_{\ell-1}}\{w^{\prime},w^{\prime\prime}\}, i.e., all the appended pendants but the dummy ones become active for the next iteration.

We conclude the construction with the completion stage 2​L+12L+1, where we append a dummy vertex dwd_{w} to every active vertex w∈ALw\in A_{L}. This construction is summarized in Table 1 and illustrated in Figure 4.

Every edge after the first attaches a new leaf. A vertex has degree at most two when it becomes active and subsequently receives at most two further incident edges. Hence TLT_{L} is a growing tree of maximum degree at most four.

To analyze this construction, we relate the matching formed by any algorithm to a vertex cover that bounds its competitiveness from above. To do so, we denote as HiH_{i} the tree after stage ii (for i∈{0,…,2​L+1}i\in\{0,\ldots,2L+1\}), i.e., HiH_{i} is the subtree of TLT_{L} consisting of edges e∈E⁡(TL)e\in E(T_{L}) with stage⁡(e)≤i\mathrm{stage}(e)\leq i. Let ALGi\mathrm{ALG}_{i} and OPTi\mathrm{OPT}_{i} be the value of the fractional matching algorithm and the size of a maximum matching of HiH_{i}. We introduce a sequence of parameters b0≥b1≥…≥b2​L+1>b2​L+2=0b_{0}\geq b_{1}\geq\ldots\geq b_{2L+1}>b_{2L+2}=0, to be chosen later, that we refer to as stage values. Write S=2​L+1S=2L+1 and λi=bi−bi+1\lambda_{i}=b_{i}-b_{i+1} for i∈{0,…,S}i\in\{0,\ldots,S\}. We will assign a nonnegative cover weight yvy_{v} to each vertex vv. We will maintain the invariant that for every stage ii and every edge u​vuv in HiH_{i} it holds that

yu+yv≥bi​.y_{u}+y_{v}\ \geq\ b_{i}\text{.} (9)

For every ii with bi>0b_{i}>0, the weights yv/biy_{v}/b_{i} satisfy the vertex-cover LP constraints from Section 4 on HiH_{i}. Our proof follows the LP-duality approach of Gamlath et al. [12, Section 2], combining matching feasibility with competitive guarantees at stage boundaries. Baligács et al. [1, Section 3.2] use a related argument for incremental vertex cover.

Lemma 12.

Under condition (9), any fractional matching algorithm satisfying ALGi≥c⋅OPTi\mathrm{ALG}_{i}\geq c\cdot\mathrm{OPT}_{i} after every stage satisfies

c≤∑v∈V⁡(TL)yv∑i=0Sλi​OPTi​.c\leq\frac{\sum_{v\in V(T_{L})}y_{v}}{\sum_{i=0}^{S}\lambda_{i}\mathrm{OPT}_{i}}\text{.} (10)

6.1 Assignment of stage values and cover weights

To complete the argument, it remains to choose the stage values b0,…,b2​L+1b_{0},\ldots,b_{2L+1} and assign values yvy_{v} appropriately. We are now ready to restate and prove our hardness result. See 3

Proof.

Consider a cc-competitive fractional matching algorithm in the edge arrival model, run on TLT_{L} with edges presented in the order of the construction stages. By Lemma 12, it holds that c≤∑v∈V⁡(TL)yv∑i=02​L+1λi​OPTic\leq\frac{\sum_{v\in V(T_{L})}y_{v}}{\sum_{i=0}^{2L+1}\lambda_{i}\mathrm{OPT}_{i}}. From Table 3, we get ∑v∈V⁡(TL)yv=2+2​L\sum_{v\in V(T_{L})}y_{v}=2+2L and ∑i=02​L+1λi​OPTi=3+72​L\sum_{i=0}^{2L+1}\lambda_{i}\mathrm{OPT}_{i}=3+\frac{7}{2}L. Thus c≤2+2​L3+72​L=4​(L+1)7​L+6c\leq\frac{2+2L}{3+\frac{7}{2}L}=\frac{4(L+1)}{7L+6}. For every c>4/7c>4/7, choose LL sufficiently large that 4​(L+1)7​L+6<c\frac{4(L+1)}{7L+6}<c. Hence no fractional matching algorithm can satisfy the competitive guarantee at every prefix of this fixed input. For a randomized algorithm, its expected edge weights form a fractional matching, so the same argument applies.∎

Incremental matching.

The hardness bound also holds when the entire edge arrival sequence is known in advance, provided that matching decisions remain irrevocable and the competitive guarantee is required after every prefix. Indeed, the proof of Lemma 12 uses only the feasibility of the fixed edge weights, not how they were chosen. Together with Theorems 1 and 2, this gives the optimal ratio 4/74/7 for fractional and randomized matching on forests in the analogue of the incremental model studied by Baligács et al. [1]. For comparison, they prove an optimal ratio of 3/23/2 for incremental fractional vertex cover; offline matching–cover duality does not imply reciprocal competitive ratios for these evolving solutions.

AI methodology.

We used AI agents to assist with the research and preparation of this paper, primarily models from the ChatGPT and Claude suites, with occasional use of DeepSeek 3.1-Flash and Xiaomi MiMo-v2.6-pro. Notably, the results described in Sections 4, 5, and 6 were discovered by AI agents after significant guidance and refined by the authors to be as simple and clear as possible. The authors have verified the correctness and originality of the results and the accuracy of the references.
